prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength bring optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from IceCube (B012) to optical lattice clocks (B007) as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. My criterion is still that the discovery comes first and the people second, and IceCube remains the stronger discovery in the sense of a clue from nature. But a prize also has to be one the committee can defend in a sentence and attribute to at most three people, and on that test the first-round exchange has moved me. The lattice clock rests on a distinct enabling idea, the magic wavelength that cancels the light shift so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, and not only on a better version of an old tool. The result has been reproduced and compared across independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) at about 1e-18, so the confirmation question is answered. The downstream use is concrete and has already begun: laboratory-scale gravitational redshift at the centimetre level, limits on varying constants and on dark-matter couplings, and the route to redefining the second. The credit is the cleanest on the list, with Katori for the concept and early strontium realisation and Ye for taking it to the accuracy and many-body frontier. Six of the eight members converge on this exact pair, and I judge that convergence on the scientific record they cite and not on the count.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not dismiss them. The 2005 prize (comb, precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (ion control) overlap, and a sceptic can read the lattice clock as a seven-order improvement of a measured quantity and not as a new phenomenon, with the new-physics tests still mostly prospective. Priority outside the pair (Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov and the ion-clock groups) is unverified, and several of us, myself included, are working from recollection of the 2001-2003 record. The redefinition of the second has not happened. Against my own earlier preference, B012 loses nothing in scientific substance by this choice: the diffuse flux remains a decade-old, solid discovery, source identification is still near four sigma, and the credit among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida, AMANDA and DUMAND is not settled. I think the committee should return to IceCube in a later year, after KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD or IceCube-Gen2 results and after outside reports on priority.

responses.point: Kroll supports B007 as a distinct enabling idea but states the overlap with 2005 and 2012 as the main objection, would accept B012 only in a pairing within three people, and flags that he relies on memory for the magic-wavelength priority record.
responses.response: In round 1 I put almost the same objection to B007, that this is an improvement of a measured quantity and not a new phenomenon, and I credit your answer that the magic-wavelength scheme is a separate step with its own stability advantage. I now treat the overlap as a matter of citation wording and not as a bar. The citation should name the neutral-atom lattice at a magic wavelength explicitly, so that it cannot be read as a second prize for the comb or for ion control. On your pairing idea, I agree with your arithmetic: Katori and Ye already use two of three seats, so a second part for IceCube would leave one name, and I would not credit Halzen or Karle alone while the Karle-Halzen-Yoshida and AMANDA questions are open. I therefore withdraw B012 as a second part for this year.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to the lattice clock for the same allocation problem I flagged, and asks whether Eriksson, Mehlig or Johansson have a scientific objection to B012 or simply less familiarity.
responses.response: I answer the chair's question as the other member who ranked B012 first. I have no scientific objection from the colleagues to report, and the physics stands. What moves me is that you and I agree on the diagnosis: the diffuse flux is a discovery, but a two- or three-name credit with a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, and a four-sigma source story is harder to write than for the clock. Given that, I prefer to say plainly that I am following the evidence on attribution, not simply the majority. Your own point that the SI redefinition is not decisive seems right to me. A clock whose 1e-18 performance is already independently compared is not made less of a result by the timing of a metrological convention.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B032 (fluctuation theorems) first on scientific grounds, argues that exact relations tested for thirty years are mature, and concedes that priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert cannot be settled in three names.
responses.response: Your point that the others have not engaged with the substance of B032 is fair, and as a theorist I find the exact relations elegant. My difficulty is the one you name yourself. A theorem that is later confirmed in pulling and trap experiments is a different kind of result from a discovery that nature forced on us, and the attribution problem is worse than for either B007 or B012, since Crooks, Cohen, Morriss and Searles would be left out. I would not wish to settle that priority history from memory. If the committee wants a statistical-physics prize in a later year, outside expert reports on the priority question would have to come first. This year I cannot put it ahead of B007, and I note that you list B007 as your first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from his opening choice of DMFT (B018) to B007, and keeps B005 (twisted bilayer graphene) and B018 as alternatives while noting the open pairing mechanism and the Metzner omission.
responses.response: I read your move to B007 on the grounds of independent confirmation and clean attribution as sound, and it is the reasoning that moved me too. On B005 I still disagree with how heavily you weigh the unsettled pairing mechanism, since the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle followed by correlated insulators and superconductivity in the lab is the arc I value, and the cuprates were honoured before their mechanism was understood. I agree with you on credit: the Cao experiments and Metzner for B018 show why neither is ready as a three-name configuration this year. I therefore keep B005 only as my second alternative, as a candidate for a future year, not as a second part now.

uncertainties: Whether the 2001-2003 priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstrations supports Katori and Ye alone, or whether Lemonde, Derevianko or Pal'chikov would have to be considered; I rely on recollection and would want the atomic-physics members and outside experts to check it.
Whether the committee will accept the citation wording as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, given that ion clocks reach comparable accuracy.

Whether a prize for a measurement and instrument is the right use of a year when a discovery of a new window on the universe (IceCube) is available but harder to credit; I have decided for B007 but the question remains open for later years.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would be wiser; I judge it is not necessary, but the committee may disagree.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen in the round-1 exchange. My ties are to David Gross (PhD supervisor), Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group, none of which touches Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted candidate, and I have no known connection to the IceCube collaboration. I note the disclosures of Olsson (Tokyo, institutional only), Johansson and Kroll (B044) and Lindroth (B003), none of which affects the preferred configuration.
